intro: The first movement of Mahler’s Symphony No. 4, marked “Bedächtig. Nicht eilen”, opens with sleigh bells, and the violins then begin a tune in G major. Later its melodies overlap and the trumpets play a fanfare.

sections.label: A · Sleigh bells and violin theme
sections.mNote: Clipped flute notes, then a leisurely theme in G major.

sections.label: B · The cellos sing in D major
Dev · Bells and fragmented themes
sections.mNote: Flute figures and the opening melody combine in minor keys.

sections.label: Dev · Trumpet theme and full-orchestra dissonance
sections.mNote: The trumpets play a melody that ends on a dissonant chord.

sections.label: A′ · Violin theme returns in G major
sections.mNote: The G major theme returns after the fanfares.

sections.label: Coda · First theme and close
sections.mNote: The opening phrases build to a quick ending.

relations.basis: The broad second theme moves from the exposition’s D major into G major in the recapitulation. A five-semitone upward pitch-class shift agrees with that home-key return. cues.title: Opening, flutes and sleigh bells
cues.text: Flutes play above sleigh bells. The violins enter with a short upward figure and continue into a tune in G major, while the lower strings play pizzicato beneath them. Mahler marks the melody Recht gemächlich, very leisurely.
cues.evidence: Mahler, Symphony No. 4, full score, opening page, printed p. 231: flutes, sleigh bells, violin entry and pizzicato accompaniment. https://s9.imslp.org/files/imglnks/usimg/4/40/IMSLP70999-PMLP58739-Mahler_-_Symphony_No._4_(orch._score).pdf
cues.how: Placed from the score; the timing is approximate.

cues.title: Bad Aussee, summer 1899
cues.text: At Bad Aussee in the summer of 1899, poor weather and the resort’s music kept Mahler from composing. He began the Fourth near the end of his holiday and worked fast. He finished the symphony at Maiernigg in August 1900.
cues.evidence: Bettie Jo Basinger, Utah Symphony guide, work history: https://usuo.org/explore/2015/05/mahler-4-listening-guide/ . Completion at Maiernigg in August 1900 is documented at https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Symphony_No._4_(Mahler)

cues.title: Second theme, cellos
cues.text: The cellos play the second theme, in D major. Its long notes follow the short turns and scales of the violins. Mahler marks the melody Breit gesungen (broadly sung).
cues.evidence: Basinger describes the cello second theme and Breit gesungen: https://usuo.org/explore/2015/05/mahler-4-listening-guide/ . Its D-major key is documented in the score and at https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Symphony_No._4_(Mahler)
cues.how: Placed from the score; the timing is approximate.

cues.title: Origin of the finale, 1892
cues.text: In 1892 Mahler wrote Das himmlische Leben, a song about heaven’s food and music, in piano and orchestral versions dated February and March. He considered it for the Third Symphony, then made it the finale of the Fourth, so the song was several years older than the movements that come before it.
cues.evidence: Basinger dates the song’s piano and orchestral versions to February and March 1892 and traces its changing place in Mahler’s plans: https://usuo.org/explore/2015/05/mahler-4-listening-guide/

cues.title: Development, minor-mode opening
cues.text: The opening flute figure returns in the minor, combined with fragments of the violin tune. The horns play the small descending triplets with sudden force. Over a low rumble in the strings a new flute melody rises, with a hint of the song from the finale.
cues.evidence: Basinger’s first-movement guide describes the development’s minor-mode opening, horn triplets, low strings and new flute melody: https://usuo.org/explore/2015/05/mahler-4-listening-guide/
cues.how: Placed from the score; the timing is approximate.

cues.title: Letter to Georg Göhler, 1911
cues.text: In 1911 Mahler wrote to Georg Göhler: “Each of the three movements is joined thematically with the last one in a most intimate and meaningful way.”
cues.evidence: Mahler to Georg Göhler concerning his 1911 essay on the Fourth; the letter is quoted in Basinger’s work history: https://usuo.org/explore/2015/05/mahler-4-listening-guide/

cues.title: Development, trumpet melody and fanfares
cues.text: In the development the melody passes to the trumpet in the major. A dissonant chord from the orchestra cuts it off. Trumpets and horns then play military fanfares.
cues.evidence: Basinger describes the major-mode trumpet melody, dissonant interruption and ensuing trumpet and horn fanfares: https://usuo.org/explore/2015/05/mahler-4-listening-guide/
cues.how: Placed from the score; the timing is approximate.

cues.title: Recapitulation, first theme
cues.text: The first theme returns quietly in G major, with its details changed. A jubilant continuation follows, and then the broad cello tune returns.
cues.evidence: Basinger describes the modified first theme, jubilant continuation and return of the second theme in the recapitulation: https://usuo.org/explore/2015/05/mahler-4-listening-guide/
cues.how: Placed from the score; the timing is approximate.

cues.title: Closing theme and coda
cues.text: Fragments of the first theme enter the quiet closing theme. They grow into the coda and its lively conclusion. The violin tune ends the movement.
cues.evidence: Basinger describes first-theme fragments entering the ruhig closing tune and growing into the coda’s lively conclusion: https://usuo.org/explore/2015/05/mahler-4-listening-guide/
cues.how: Placed from the score; the timing is approximate.

transitions.title: Transition to D major and cello theme
transitions.from: A · Sleigh bells and violin theme
transitions.to: B · The cellos sing in D major
transitions.how: The continuation of the first theme, with turns and short scales in the violins, accelerates towards D major, the dominant of G. The cellos then take the second theme in long notes in a lower register, marked Breit gesungen.
transitions.evidence: Basinger’s account of the accelerating transition and cello second theme: https://usuo.org/explore/2015/05/mahler-4-listening-guide/ . D-major key: https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Symphony_No._4_(Mahler)

transitions.title: The flute figure turns to minor
transitions.from: B · The cellos sing in D major
transitions.how: The exposition returns to G major and its quiet closing tune. The development brings back the opening flute figure in the minor and combines it with pieces of the first theme. The horns take up the tune’s descending triplets.
transitions.evidence: Basinger, first-movement guide, exposition ending and development opening: https://usuo.org/explore/2015/05/mahler-4-listening-guide/

transitions.title: Dissonant chord cuts across the trumpet
transitions.to: Dev · Trumpet theme and full-orchestra dissonance
transitions.how: The development melody moves into the major and passes to the trumpet. A dissonant chord in the full orchestra cuts across it. The massed winds and strings then drop out, leaving military fanfares in the trumpets and horns.
transitions.evidence: Basinger describes the trumpet statement, dissonant interruption and fanfare aftermath: https://usuo.org/explore/2015/05/mahler-4-listening-guide/

transitions.title: From the fanfares to the recapitulation
transitions.from: Dev · Trumpet theme and full-orchestra dissonance
transitions.to: A′ · Violin theme returns in G major
transitions.how: The trumpet and horn calls die away. The strings play a quiet, altered version of the first theme, and the key returns to G major. The familiar phrase of the theme takes the place of the isolated fanfares, and the cymbals then mark the start of a more jubilant continuation.
transitions.evidence: Basinger, transition from the fanfares to the recapitulation and its cymbal-led expansion: https://usuo.org/explore/2015/05/mahler-4-listening-guide/

transitions.title: Closing theme and first-theme fragments into coda
transitions.from: A′ · Violin theme returns in G major
transitions.how: The quiet closing melody returns in G major, and small phrases from the first violin tune appear within it. These fragments carry the music into the coda. The orchestral texture thins, then the full orchestra returns for the quick final bars.
transitions.evidence: Basinger’s account of the ruhig closing theme and first-theme fragments that become the coda: https://usuo.org/explore/2015/05/mahler-4-listening-guide/

source.title: Mahler, Symphony No. 4, I. Bedächtig, full score
source.locator: First movement, pp. 231–274, rehearsal figures 1–23: sleigh-bell opening, cello second theme, trumpet outburst and returning violin tune.

timeline.note: Flutes and sleigh bells frame the first violin tune; winds answer its turns and short figures.
Cellos begin the broadly sung second theme; violins continue its long line above soft wind harmony.
Woodwinds trade short phrases above lighter string figures after the broad cello melody.
Bells and flute figures return; horns and divided strings pass fragments through the development.
High wind phrases, horn calls and quick string lines overlap, with harp and percussion between them.
The trumpet melody rises above winds and strings before a harsh orchestral chord interrupts it.
Trumpet and horn fanfares enter as the strings recede; soft woodwind figures answer.
The violin theme returns over pizzicato inner strings, with answering phrases in the horn and woodwind.
The broad lyrical line returns in the strings, supported by wind chords and sustained horns.
Low clarinet figures and quiet strings bring back fragments of the opening in the closing pages. The bells return briefly.
Strings and upper winds play the quick close; horns, trumpet, timpani, triangle and cymbals reinforce it.

composer.epithet: Conductor who composed during the summers and intended each symphony to contain a whole world, combining the sublime with the music of the street band.
facts: Vienna Conservatory, 1875–78: piano with Julius Epstein, composition with Franz Krenn; attended Bruckner’s university lectures
Budapest Royal Opera 1888–91 · Hamburg Stadttheater 1891–97 · Vienna Court Opera 1897–1907 · Metropolitan Opera and New York Philharmonic 1908–11
In summer huts at Steinbach am Attersee, Maiernigg on the Wörthersee and Toblach in the Dolomites
Nine numbered symphonies and an unfinished Tenth; Das Lied von der Erde; orchestral songs

quote.text: The symphony must be like the world. It must embrace everything.
quote.source: To Jean Sibelius, Helsinki, 1907, as Sibelius remembered it

composer.background:
Mahler was born in a Bohemian village and grew up in the garrison town of Iglau (Jihlava), the second of fourteen children, eight of whom died young. In Iglau he heard bugle calls and marches from the barracks, Czech and German folk song, the town band, the synagogue and the Catholic church, and these sounds recur throughout his music. Late in life he told Sigmund Freud that he had once run from a violent quarrel between his parents into the street, where a barrel organ was playing Ach, du lieber Augustin.

At fifteen he entered the Vienna Conservatory, where he studied piano and composition, and he sat in on Bruckner’s harmony lectures at the University. Among his friends were Hugo Wolf and Hans Rott, who died young. Rott’s symphony is so close to Mahler’s own music that Mahler later called Rott the founder of the new symphony as he understood it. The cantata Das klagende Lied, completed in 1880, failed to win the Beethoven Prize in 1881. By then he had already begun his career as a conductor.
